segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That evening Jory Brennick sat on the Floatsome platform coiling dive line by the last of the light, and said the rule out loud again, because saying it was the only way he could think of to keep hold of it.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: The name three times. In open air. Never under the water. So the box comes up first, whole, with nobody speaking a word over it until it's on the deck.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud Brennick was sat across from him with a torn net over her knees and a shuttle in her hand, and she did not look up.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: And the plate was warm.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Through a wet glove. I've had my hand on cold iron down there for twenty years of my life and it takes the feeling out of you in a minute. That plate gave the feeling back.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The shuttle stopped. Maud held it where it was, halfway through a mesh, and looked past her son at the dark water beyond the lashed hulls.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: I was eleven the autumn after the flood. We were in the camp above the shoreline then, the one that burned twice. Boats went out over the old streets all that season. Everybody rowing out to float over their own roof and see what the water had left of it.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Salvaging.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Grieving, mostly. They stopped by the turn of the year. Cold came in, and there's nothing to bring up but furniture, and furniture isn't worth a chill. By midwinter the streets had nobody over them at all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She set the shuttle down on the boards.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Except one. There was an old woman rowed out alone, three and four nights a week, and a lantern stood in her bow. Kettle Row, the short end, over the dyers. I know it was that corner because I used to lie on the boards and watch the light sit still on the water. A lantern on a boat moves. Hers didn't. She'd tie up and work and the light would hold in one place half the night.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Nobody asked her what she was at?

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: People asked. She wasn't a woman who answered. What they said about her instead was the fever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Liora Quill had come along the walkway with her boots in her hand, and stopped where she was.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: It went through the camps that first winter and took the old and the small ones first, the way they do. Then it stopped taking them. The talk was that there was a draught going round, and that it came off an old woman from the drowned town, and that children who'd gone grey in the face sat up and asked for bread. I never drank it. My mother did.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: And nobody wrote down how she made it?

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Nobody got the chance. She stopped coming round in the spring. One season she was rowing out, and the next she wasn't, and people had roofs to put on.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jory looked at the coil in his hands and did not finish it.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Here's what I want you holding tomorrow. That stone came up out of the seabed six months before she worked it. Nobody knew what it was. Nobody knows now. She made that lock once, shut it once, and no hand has opened it since. Whatever it takes off the one who speaks, there's not a living soul who has watched it taken.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Walter Ames knows that. He read it to us himself.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Reading a thing and standing on a wet deck saying your own name to it are different trades.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Feet came along the outer walkway at a run. It was a Shoreside boy, soaked to the knee, with his cap screwed up in his fist, and he got the message out in one breath because he had plainly been given it in one.

segments.speaker: Liora Quill
segments.text: Say that again. Slower.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The boy swallowed and said it again.

segments.speaker: Jory Brennick
segments.text: Two days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Maud picked the shuttle back up off the boards.

segments.speaker: Maud Brennick
segments.text: Then we go at first light, and we go the three of us, and your old man stays in the boat with his letter.
